description: We want to grow Arab Space Exploration!
summary:
Tether is a daily health check for astronauts on long missions. In about a minute a crew member logs eight readings: sleep, mood, resting heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood glucose, body mass and exercise. Tether compares each one with that person's own pre-flight baseline instead of a population average, and shows the result as one score with three states: Steady, Drifting and Off baseline.

It then answers the question a number alone cannot: who needs to act. A single off day is the crew member's to handle. A three-day trend, or two body systems drifting together, goes to the crew medical officer. Any reading past a safety limit goes to the flight surgeon. Because a reply from Earth can take 20 minutes on the way to Mars, Tether lists what to do while waiting.

This matters because the farther a crew travels, the less they can lean on ground doctors. Tether ties five body systems to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, tracks radiation dose against NASA's career limit, and keeps working with no link to Earth.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Tether is a web app a crew member opens once a day. A new user sets up a profile (name, role, mission, mission day and pre-flight baseline) or explores a demo crew member on day 142 of a Mars transit.

The check-in asks for eight readings, one per screen. Each screen explains how to take that measurement without gravity and why it matters in flight. A heart-rate band can fill in its step over Bluetooth.

The Today screen shows one score from 0 to 100 and one of three states. Each state has its own colour, shape and word, so it reads without colour vision. A body map places five systems (mind, immune, heart, metabolism, bone and muscle) on a figure, each tied to one of NASA's five hazards. Trend charts show every reading against the crew member's own normal range.

HOW IT WORKS

Every indicator has a personal baseline: a mean and a normal day-to-day swing. A reading is Drifting when it is 1.75 or more swings from baseline, or past a caution limit. It is Off baseline at three or more swings, or past a fixed safety limit that applies to anyone, such as a temperature of 38.0 °C. Sleep, mood, resting heart rate and exercise are judged on a three-day average so one bad night does not raise a flag.

Plain rules then set the plan: handle it yourself, tell the crew medical officer, or contact the flight surgeon. The user picks the mission (space station, lunar surface, Mars transit, Mars surface) and the signal delay changes the advice. The app also tracks cumulative radiation dose for the mission against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.

An assistant called Ask Tether sits at the bottom of every screen. It suggests questions from the crew member's current state and answers from their own readings. It only explains. It is given the readings and the plan the rules already produced, and is instructed not to invent numbers, diagnose, or soften the plan. With a link to the ground it uses Google Gemini; without one it answers from the on-board rules.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A crew member far from Earth has to judge their own health. Tether turns a set of readings into one decision and names who should act, which lowers the chance that a slow trend is missed or that a serious reading waits for a reply. Because no model decides a status or a plan, every recommendation can be traced to the reading and the limit that caused it.

WHAT WE USED

React, TypeScript and Vite, with plain CSS. Charts and the body figure are hand-written SVG. The site and the assistant's endpoint run on Cloudflare Pages. The assistant uses the Google Gemini API. Wearables connect through the Web Bluetooth heart-rate service. Profiles are stored in the browser only; there are no accounts.

WHAT IS CREATIVE ABOUT IT

Tether judges each person against themselves, not an average. It answers "who acts" instead of stopping at a number. The advice changes with distance from Earth. It keeps working when the link is down.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Accessibility: every state is shown by colour, shape and word, and motion respects the reduced-motion setting. Trust: rules decide, the assistant explains. Privacy: health data stays on the device. Honesty: the demo runs on a simulated 141-day log for a fictional crew member, no real astronaut data is used, and the thresholds illustrate the approach and are not medical advice.
